tier_reason: The README Results table shows Tessera at 10.8 ms (~92M rows/s, 11.4 MB), a per-symbol binary-search join at 82.9 ms and pandas.merge_asof at 152.8 ms, with the ~14x and ~7.7x stated. The benchmark code is public (bench/Tessera.Benchmarks/Program.cs uses BenchmarkDotNet; bench/python/merge_asof_bench.py) and it runs on .NET 9 Release, but no CPU model or pandas/Python version is given, so the tier stays at C.

corrections.caveats: Very small single-author project (1 star). The repo was created 2026-06-26 and all 7 commits landed between 2026-06-26 and 2026-06-27, so the project was about a day old at its last commit, not a month. No CPU model is stated (only 'single dev laptop'; the SIMD section says AVX2) and the pandas, numpy and Python versions are not given, which caps evidence at tier C. The comparison is one specialized operation (a backward as-of join on presorted data with pre-factorized int symbol codes), not general dataframe performance. The pandas side is a single time.perf_counter measurement after a small warm-up, while the C# side is a BenchmarkDotNet mean, so the ~14x crosses languages and timing methods.
corrections.hardware: unstated ('single dev laptop'; the SIMD section says AVX2, 4 doubles/lane)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: .NET 9, Release configuration (BenchmarkDotNet via dotnet run -c Release); pandas/numpy/Python versions unstated

notes: The numbers match the README exactly, and the metadata checks out (MIT, 1 star, last commit 2026-06-27, not a fork). The caveat's '~1 month old' was wrong: the whole history spans about a day. The commits carry an AI co-author trailer.

tier_reason: docs/BENCHMARKS.md gives first-party numbers from 2 runs on 2M synthetic rows (6.50 vs 8.13 bytes/trade against Parquet+zstd, plus query timings against DuckDB and Polars). The harness is public (bench/compare_duckdb_parquet.py, bench/tickdb_bench_rs), but no hardware, CPU, compiler or flags are stated, so the tier is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Not faster on any speed axis. Storage: 6.50 bytes/trade vs 8.13 for Parquet+zstd, which the page itself calls 'genuinely 20% smaller'. Ingest: 7.32M rows/s (1 run) vs DuckDB CSV load at 20.05-20.67M rows/s, about 2.7x slower (the page notes tickdb's path includes WAL/durability). Queries: DuckDB wins OHLCV by ~1.5-1.6x, VWAP by ~190-240x and top-10-by-volume by ~55-115x. Polars also beats tickdb on VWAP.
corrections.workload: 2,000,000 synthetic trade rows. Measures on-disk bytes per trade (delta-of-delta timestamps, delta/zigzag prices, RLE, zstd) against Parquet written by DuckDB COPY ... (FORMAT PARQUET, COMPRESSION ZSTD); ingest vs DuckDB CSV load (1 run); and OHLCV/VWAP/top-10 query time vs DuckDB over Parquet (Polars on VWAP only). 2 runs on the author's machine, July 2026.
corrections.caveats: No license file (GitHub reports no license), so the code cannot legally be reused and usability is reference. The only win is storage footprint, ~20% smaller than DuckDB-written Parquet+zstd on synthetic data; tickdb is slower on ingest (~2.7x) and on every benchmarked query (1.5x to over 200x). The README calls it a systems-engineering portfolio project, not for production. No hardware is stated.

notes: The numbers are accurate and candidly reported, but the project is slower than its baselines on every speed axis and its only advantage is a ~20% smaller on-disk size. That makes it a not-faster scope reject, like the jsonbinpack precedent; keep it flagged with the shortcoming if policy says so. Metadata is verified: no license, 0 stars, last commit 2026-07-04, not a fork.

tier_reason: The 2020-09-15 Cockroach Labs post (Peter Mattis) compares Pebble with RocksDB on YCSB in two unlabeled bar charts: a 3-node CockroachDB cluster on A-F and a storage-engine-only run on A-E. The YCSB tool is public (cmd/pebble/ycsb.go), but no CPU, instance type, Go/RocksDB versions or flags are given. That is first-party with partial methodology, so tier C.

corrections.hardware: Not specified. The post gives no CPU, instance type or node spec for the charted runs; its AWS/GCP mention refers to the nightly roachtest integration suite, not to these benchmarks. The CockroachDB-level chart is titled '3-node CockroachDB cluster'.
corrections.workload: YCSB workloads A-F at the CockroachDB level (3-node cluster), plus a storage-engine-only YCSB tool run directly on Pebble and RocksDB for A-E only (workload F was not implemented there). Engines were configured with similar options, identical where they overlapped. Datasets fit in memory; out-of-cache testing is mentioned but not shown. The post does not state the key distribution.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Text: 'Pebble meets or exceeds RocksDB on the 6 standard YCSB workloads'; the large workload C gap is attributed to better concurrency in Pebble's block and table caches. Chart bars (unlabeled y-axis, approximate readings, derived from page data): at the CockroachDB level, about 21k vs 22.5k (A), 38k vs 40.5k (B), 54k vs 57k (C), 42.5k vs 45k (D), tie at ~6k (E), 9.5k vs 9.8k (F), so about 0-7%. Storage engine only: about 690k vs 860k (A), 750k vs 980k (B), 860k vs 1.6M (C, ~1.85x), 720k vs 890k (D), 185k vs 235k (E), so about 1.2-1.3x except C.
corrections.caveats: The numbers exist only as unlabeled bar charts in a 2020-09-15 vendor post, and the post names no CPU, instance type, Go or RocksDB version, or flags, so it falls short of tier A/B. The YCSB harness is public (cmd/pebble/ycsb.go in the Pebble repo). The storage-only comparison skips workload F. At the CockroachDB level the gain is small (about 0-7%, E tied) because other bottlenecks dominate. The measurements are six years old, and both engines have changed a lot since.

notes: The claim is accurate and conservative.
